transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Lately I can’t seem to focus at work—my mind keeps drifting back to everything that could go wrong with my job. It has just been really hard to keep my attention on what I'm doing when I'm constantly worrying about what might happen next.
How long have you been feeling this way, and did it start after a specific stressful event at work or in your life?

It’s been going on pretty steadily for about nine months now. It all started when my clinic announced a major reorganization, which brought a lot of uncertainty about my future role and led to several of my long-time coworkers leaving.

Are you still dealing with the job reorganization and uncertainty now, or has that situation mostly resolved? Since this started, has your worry stayed mainly about that work stressor, or has it spread to many other parts of your life too?

Yes, the reorganization is still completely unresolved, so that stress is ongoing. The worry has definitely spread to other areas too—I find myself constantly stressing about paying rent, and I've even had to pull back from my photography and art workshops because my mind is always stuck in a loop of "what-ifs."

On most days over these nine months, have you felt excessive worry about several different areas of life that is hard to control even when work stress isn’t the main issue? Or does your anxiety mostly rise in direct response to the ongoing job reorganization and its consequences?

My anxiety is really rooted in the ongoing reorganization and its consequences. My mind constantly jumps between worries like being demoted, failing if I get promoted, or not being able to pay rent if my hours change. Once those thoughts start, it feels like a loop I just can't control or shut off, no matter how hard I try to distract myself.

If the job reorganization were resolved and your role felt secure again, do you think your anxiety would mostly go away, or would you still be worrying excessively about many other parts of life? Has this kind of hard-to-control worry ever happened before this work stress began?

I'm not entirely sure if the worry would completely go away, though I'd like to hope things would get better if my job felt secure again. As for the past, I don't recall ever experiencing this level of uncontrollable worry before all this work stress started.

Aside from the worry itself, have these symptoms caused clear problems in your daily life—like sleep trouble, muscle tension, or irritability—and do they feel out of proportion to the job reorganization? Or do they seem like a direct reaction that fits the stress you’re under?

Yes, it has caused major problems—I'm constantly tense, barely sleep because I'm replaying the day, and I've been making scheduling mistakes at work and pulling back from my art workshops. It definitely feels out of proportion, as even a minor typo in an email makes me spiral into worrying that I'll lose my job, and I just can't shut the thoughts off.

When your mind isn’t focused on the job reorganization, do you still spend a lot of the day worrying excessively about other unrelated things? Or is the anxiety mainly tied to the work situation and what could happen because of it?

The anxiety is almost entirely tied to the work reorganization and the chain reaction of worries it causes. My mind just jumps between fears like being demoted, failing if I'm promoted, or not being able to pay rent if my hours change. Even when I try to distract myself with my photography, I quickly loop right back to worrying about the clinic's schedule.

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began in clear temporal relation to an identifiable psychosocial stressor (ongoing workplace reorganization), are predominantly centered on that stressor and its consequences, and have caused distress and functional impairment. Although the worry is excessive and hard to control with insomnia and tension, it does not appear to be free-floating across multiple domains independent of the stressor, making adjustment disorder more fitting than generalized anxiety disorder.
